The 2000s were Hollywood's last traditional decade. This is not nostalgia talking. The data backs it up. Of the 44 major films VirtueVigil has reviewed and scored from the aughts, 40 score TRADITIONAL or better. Two land in MIXED territory. Only two cross into WOKE territory -- and one of those is Avatar, a 2009 release that functions, in retrospect, as the decade's closing argument about where the industry was heading. The 2000s did not have a Fight Club problem or a Pulp Fiction problem. It had a volume problem: the sheer number of films that scored +20, +30, even +40 on the TRAD margin is something no subsequent decade has matched.

This was the decade when Hollywood still believed in heroism without irony. The Lord of the Rings trilogy, Gladiator, Batman Begins, The Dark Knight, United 93, Black Hawk Down -- these are films built on the conviction that courage, sacrifice, and duty are real things, not constructs to be deconstructed. Peter Jackson opened the decade with Fellowship and closed it with Return of the King winning eleven Oscars, a number that still seems impossible for a fantasy trilogy about hobbits and honor. Pixar was at its creative peak: The Incredibles and Up are among the most traditional animated films ever produced by a major studio, both scoring beyond +23 TRAD. The 2000s were the last moment when the industry's biggest swings -- its Oscar bait, its blockbusters, its prestige television -- were aligned with what audiences actually valued.

But the transition was underway. The late 2000s brought WALL-E (MIXED, +1.2), The Hurt Locker (WOKE LEAN, -3.9), and Avatar (WOKE, -12.5). The ingredients that would define the 2010s -- environmental messaging, anti-war deconstruction, the elevation of identity over story -- were simmering beneath the surface. The 2000s were not the 1990s, where only four of thirty films fell outside TRADITIONAL territory. The center was holding, but the cracks were visible to anyone paying attention. What follows is the definitive ranking of the decade's most significant films by ideological content. Forty-four movies, scored and ranked, from the strongest traditional to the most woke. Every film links to the full VirtueVigil review with complete category breakdowns.

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL

#1. The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 64.5 WOKE: 0.3 MARGIN: +64.1 TRAD

Director: Peter Jackson • Stars: Elijah Wood (Frodo), Ian McKellen (Gandalf), Viggo Mortensen (Aragorn), Sean Astin (Samwise), Andy Serkis (Gollum), Orlando Bloom (Legolas), Cate Blanchett (Galadriel) • Year: 2003

At +64.1 TRAD, The Return of the King is the most traditional film VirtueVigil has ever scored, and by a margin so large it constitutes its own category. The 0.3 woke score is functionally zero: there is virtually nothing in this film that a progressive ideological framework can claim. Aragorn's arc is the restoration of rightful kingship, not its deconstruction. Frodo's failure at the Cracks of Doom -- he claims the Ring rather than destroying it -- is the most theologically sophisticated moment in blockbuster cinema: evil is not defeated by human willpower but by providential irony, Gollum's oath-breaking leading to his unwitting completion of the quest. Samwise Gamgee is the film's moral center, a gardener who carries his master up a volcano when the master can no longer walk. The multiple endings, often criticized, are structurally necessary: they show that victory does not erase cost. Frodo is too wounded to remain in the Shire. He sails into the West. That is not a happy ending. It is an honest one. Eleven Academy Awards, $1.1 billion at the box office, and the most ideologically traditional major film Hollywood has ever produced.

#2. The Passion of the Christ (2004)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 45.3 WOKE: 0.0 MARGIN: +45.3 TRAD

Director: Mel Gibson • Stars: Jim Caviezel (Jesus), Monica Bellucci (Magdalen), Maia Morgenstern (Mary) • Year: 2004

The Passion of the Christ earned a 0.0 woke score, the lowest VirtueVigil has ever recorded. There is simply nothing in this film for a progressive framework to work with. Gibson's film is a literal, unflinching, Aramaic-and-Latin depiction of the final twelve hours of Jesus Christ's life, and it refuses every modern sensibility about what religious art should be. The violence is not stylized. It is excruciating. The film made $612 million against a $30 million budget despite every studio in Hollywood passing on it. The audience was there. The gatekeepers were wrong. Gibson self-financed, cast an actor few Americans had heard of, and delivered a film that operates entirely within a pre-modern moral universe: sacrifice, redemption, the weight of sin, the reality of evil, the necessity of suffering. The 0.0 is not a rounding error. It is a statement about what happens when a filmmaker refuses to negotiate with the reigning ideology.

#3. Miracle (2004)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 37.4 WOKE: 1.4 MARGIN: +36.0 TRAD

Director: Gavin O'Connor • Stars: Kurt Russell (Herb Brooks), Patricia Clarkson (Patti Brooks), Noah Emmerich (Craig Patrick) • Year: 2004

Miracle is the best sports film of the 2000s, and it accomplishes something almost no other film in the genre manages: it makes you feel the weight of what the 1980 U.S. Olympic hockey team actually did. Herb Brooks, played by Kurt Russell in a career-best performance, is not a warm coach. He is a man who understands that greatness requires cruelty, that the Soviet machine will not be beaten by talent alone, and that twenty college kids from Minnesota and Massachusetts need to hate him before they can become a team. The film's famous pre-game speech is not rah-rah. It is a cold strategic assessment followed by a single sentence: "You were born to be hockey players. Every one of you." The Cold War framing is not subtext. It is text. America versus the Soviet Union. Freedom versus coercion. Individual will versus the collective. The film never apologizes for this framing because it does not occur to anyone involved that there is anything to apologize for. +36.0 TRAD.

#4. The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 36.1 WOKE: 0.3 MARGIN: +35.8 TRAD

Director: Peter Jackson • Stars: Elijah Wood (Frodo), Ian McKellen (Gandalf), Viggo Mortensen (Aragorn), Sean Astin (Samwise), Sean Bean (Boromir) • Year: 2001

Fellowship opens the trilogy with the most sustained moral argument in blockbuster cinema: that the smallest person can change the course of the future, not through power but through willingness. The Council of Elrond is the scene where the entire trilogy's moral architecture is laid out. Every great power in Middle-earth argues about who should carry the Ring. Frodo, a hobbit who has never held a sword, volunteers. He does not understand what he is agreeing to. That is the point. Gandalf's quiet expression of relief and grief in that moment -- relief that someone stepped forward, grief at what it will cost that someone -- is the emotional thesis of the entire project. Boromir's fall and redemption at Amon Hen gives the film its tragic dimension: he tries to take the Ring, fails, and dies defending Merry and Pippin, confessing to Aragorn that he would have followed him as king. The traditional architecture is near-perfect. +35.8 TRAD.

#5. Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2002)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 36.7 WOKE: 4.6 MARGIN: +32.1 TRAD

Director: Chris Columbus • Stars: Daniel Radcliffe (Harry), Emma Watson (Hermione), Rupert Grint (Ron), Kenneth Branagh (Lockhart), Jason Isaacs (Lucius Malfoy) • Year: 2002

The second Potter film is the most traditional of the eight, and the reason is structural: this is a story about lineage, inheritance, and the moral content of blood. The Chamber of Secrets is opened by the heir of Slytherin, and the entire mystery turns on the question of who belongs at Hogwarts and who does not. The film's answer is that worth is not determined by parentage. Harry pulls the Sword of Gryffindor from the Sorting Hat not because he is a pureblood but because he is loyal to Dumbledore -- because he chose the right side. Dumbledore's closing line -- "It is not our abilities that show what we truly are. It is our choices" -- is the moral of the entire series in one sentence. The film is dark for a children's movie: petrified students, a murdered ghost, a giant serpent, a memory-preserved teenage Voldemort who drains Ginny's life force. It is also the film where Kenneth Branagh's Gilderoy Lockhart gives one of the great comic performances in the series as a fraud whose entire career is built on taking credit for other people's heroism. +32.1 TRAD.

#6. Gladiator (2000)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 32.2 WOKE: 1.7 MARGIN: +30.5 TRAD

Director: Ridley Scott • Stars: Russell Crowe (Maximus), Joaquin Phoenix (Commodus), Connie Nielsen (Lucilla), Oliver Reed (Proximo) • Year: 2000

Gladiator revived the sword-and-sandal epic for a generation that had never seen one, and it did so by stripping the genre to its traditional bones. Maximus Decimus Meridius is a general betrayed by a jealous emperor's son, his family murdered, himself sold into slavery, who rises through the gladiatorial ranks with one objective: to kill the man who took everything from him. The film's moral framework is Roman in the Stoic sense: duty, honor, loyalty to the dead, and the conviction that a man's soul cannot be taken from him -- only his life. Commodus is one of the great villains of the decade, a man whose father loved a general more than his own son, and whose entire reign is a tantrum about that fact. The final confrontation in the Colosseum is not a battle. It is an execution. Commodus stabs Maximus before the fight, Maximus still kills him, and dies having restored the Senate. "Go to them," he tells Lucilla of his murdered family. The gates of Elysium open. +30.5 TRAD.

#7. Band of Brothers (2001)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 29.6 WOKE: 1.1 MARGIN: +28.5 TRAD

Director: Various • Stars: Damian Lewis (Winters), Ron Livingston (Nixon), Scott Grimes (Malarkey), Donnie Wahlberg (Lipton) • Year: 2001

Band of Brothers is the finest television miniseries ever produced, and its ideological content is so traditional that the 1.1 woke score barely registers. The ten-episode arc follows Easy Company, 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division, from training at Camp Toccoa through D-Day, Operation Market Garden, the Battle of the Bulge, and the capture of Hitler's Eagle's Nest. Richard Winters is the moral center: a quiet, competent, deeply principled officer who leads from the front and never asks his men to do anything he would not do himself. The series does not glamorize war. It does not critique it either. It simply shows what happened, and the cumulative effect is an argument about leadership, loyalty, and sacrifice that no ideological framework can co-opt. The final episode -- the real veterans, now old men, speaking about who they were and what they did -- is the most emotionally devastating ten minutes in television history. +28.5 TRAD.

#8. Up (2009)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 28.6 WOKE: 2.8 MARGIN: +25.8 TRAD

Director: Pete Docter • Stars: Ed Asner (Carl), Christopher Plummer (Muntz), Jordan Nagai (Russell) • Year: 2009

The first ten minutes of Up constitute the most emotionally efficient marriage story ever put on film. Carl and Ellie meet as children, share a dream of adventure, marry, build a life, endure infertility, save for a trip they never take, and grow old together. Then she dies. It is four minutes of silent montage that reduces grown adults to tears, and there is nothing remotely woke about any of it. The film proper follows Carl, now a bitter widower, who ties thousands of balloons to his house and flies to South America to fulfill the promise he made to his wife. What he finds is that the adventure was never the point. The life they lived together was. Russell, the Wilderness Explorer who stows away on Carl's porch, is not a substitute grandson designed to teach Carl progressive lessons about found family. He is a boy who needs a father figure, and Carl, reluctantly, becomes one. The villain, Charles Muntz, is a man who sacrificed everything -- his reputation, his humanity, his dogs -- to prove he was right. The contrast is the entire moral argument of the film. +25.8 TRAD.

#9. The Incredibles (2004)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 24.9 WOKE: 1.4 MARGIN: +23.5 TRAD

Director: Brad Bird • Stars: Craig T. Nelson (Bob/Mr. Incredible), Holly Hunter (Helen/Elastigirl), Samuel L. Jackson (Frozone), Jason Lee (Syndrome) • Year: 2004

Brad Bird's The Incredibles is the most philosophically traditional Pixar film, which is saying something for a studio whose output in the 2000s was overwhelmingly traditional. The villain, Syndrome, is an aggrieved fan who was told as a child that he could not be a superhero, and whose response is to build technology that will make everyone super -- "so that no one will be." This is the ethos of enforced equality as tyranny, and the film treats it as monstrous. Bob Parr's midlife crisis is not about patriarchy. It is about a man who was built for greatness being forced to live a small life, and the film argues that excellence should be celebrated, not suppressed. Helen/Elastigirl is a wife and mother who is also a capable superhero, and the film does not pit those roles against each other. Dash's storyline -- "Everyone's special, Dash." "Which is another way of saying no one is" -- is a direct refutation of the participation-trophy culture that was already ascendant in 2004. The film ends with the family united, fighting together, each using their unique gifts. +23.5 TRAD.

#10. United 93 (2006)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 25.2 WOKE: 2.5 MARGIN: +22.8 TRAD

Director: Paul Greengrass • Stars: Christian Clemenson, Cheyenne Jackson, David Alan Basche • Year: 2006

United 93 is the most difficult film on this list to watch, and the most important. Paul Greengrass reconstructed the events of September 11, 2001 aboard the one hijacked flight that did not reach its target, using unknown actors and a documentary-realist style that strips away every layer of Hollywood artifice. The passengers and crew of Flight 93 were ordinary people who, over the course of 81 minutes, learned through phone calls what had happened in New York and Washington, understood that their plane was part of the same attack, and chose to fight back. They rushed the cockpit knowing they would likely die. Their sacrifice almost certainly saved the U.S. Capitol or the White House from destruction. The film does not give speeches. It does not editorialize. It presents what happened, and the moral content is inescapable: forty ordinary Americans, faced with a choice between certain death and possible death while fighting, chose to fight. +22.8 TRAD.

#11. Black Hawk Down (2001)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 24.8 WOKE: 2.8 MARGIN: +22.0 TRAD

Director: Ridley Scott • Stars: Josh Hartnett (Eversmann), Ewan McGregor (Grimes), Tom Sizemore (McKnight), Eric Bana (Hoot) • Year: 2001

Ridley Scott's second entry on this list is a harrowing reconstruction of the 1993 Battle of Mogadishu, in which 160 U.S. soldiers were surrounded by thousands of Somali militiamen during what was supposed to be a one-hour mission. The film does not explain the geopolitical context. It drops you into the chaos and leaves you there. The Americans are not portrayed as imperialist invaders. They are soldiers following orders in an impossible situation, and the film's loyalty is entirely with the men on the ground. The famous "Why do you do it?" exchange -- Hoot's response that it is about the man next to you, nothing more -- is the ethos of the film in two sentences. The Rangers and Delta operators who fought through the night to reach the crash sites did so because their brothers were there. "Leave no man behind" is not a bumper sticker in this film. It is a moral imperative that costs 18 American lives and saves many more. +22.0 TRAD.

#12. The Patriot (2000)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 24.6 WOKE: 2.7 MARGIN: +21.9 TRAD

Director: Roland Emmerich • Stars: Mel Gibson (Benjamin Martin), Heath Ledger (Gabriel), Jason Isaacs (Tavington) • Year: 2000

The Patriot is the most unapologetically American film Roland Emmerich ever made, and what makes it work is Mel Gibson's Benjamin Martin, a veteran of the French and Indian War who wants nothing to do with the Revolution. He has seen what war does to men. He knows what he is capable of. He is not a reluctant hero in the conventional sense. He is a man who has already done terrible things and does not wish to do them again. When Colonel Tavington murders his son Thomas in cold blood, Martin's neutrality collapses. What follows is a war film about a father fighting alongside his surviving sons, and the film's moral calculus is refreshingly simple: the British are the aggressors, the colonists are defending their homes, and some evils require violence to answer. The final confrontation between Martin and Tavington is not a duel. It is an accounting. +21.9 TRAD.

#13. The Prestige (2006)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 21.6 WOKE: 0.0 MARGIN: +21.6 TRAD

Director: Christopher Nolan • Stars: Hugh Jackman (Angier), Christian Bale (Borden), Michael Caine (Cutter), Scarlett Johansson (Olivia) • Year: 2006

The Prestige is Christopher Nolan's masterpiece and, alongside The Passion of the Christ, one of only two films on this list with a 0.0 woke score. The film is a structural magic trick about two rival magicians in Victorian London whose obsession with outdoing each other destroys everything they love. Every element of the film's moral architecture is traditional: obsession as sin, sacrifice as the price of greatness, the distinction between the prestige (the effect) and the work (the cost). Borden lives a double life so complete that he shares his identity with his twin brother, each man living only half a life so the act can continue. Angier literally drowns himself every night, creating a new copy of himself in a machine built by Tesla, murdering the previous version. The film's famous structure -- three timelines interwoven, each reveal embedded in the next -- is not cleverness for its own sake. It is a demonstration that the audience wants to be fooled, and that being fooled has a moral cost. +21.6 TRAD.

#14. Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (2001)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 23.6 WOKE: 2.4 MARGIN: +21.2 TRAD

Director: Chris Columbus • Stars: Daniel Radcliffe (Harry), Emma Watson (Hermione), Rupert Grint (Ron), Richard Harris (Dumbledore), Alan Rickman (Snape) • Year: 2001

The film that launched the most successful literary adaptation in history, and one whose traditional foundations are so solid that they would support eight films and a generation of fans. Harry Potter is an orphan raised in a cupboard under the stairs by relatives who resent his very existence. The discovery that he is a wizard -- that his parents were heroes who died protecting him, that he is known and celebrated in a world he never knew existed -- is the most powerful wish-fulfillment fantasy in children's literature. But the film's real moral content is in the choices, not the magic. Harry refuses Draco Malfoy's offered friendship because Malfoy insults Ron. Hermione lies to protect Harry and Ron from punishment for the troll incident. Ron sacrifices himself in the giant chess match so Harry can go on. The Sorcerer's Stone, hidden in the Mirror of Erised, is only accessible to someone who wants to find it but not use it -- a test of character, not skill. +21.2 TRAD.

#15. 300 (2006)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 23.6 WOKE: 2.5 MARGIN: +21.1 TRAD

Director: Zack Snyder • Stars: Gerard Butler (Leonidas), Lena Headey (Gorgo), Dominic West (Theron), David Wenham (Dilios) • Year: 2006

300 is the most viscerally masculine film of the 2000s, and the backlash against it from critics who found it fascist or cartoonish tells you more about the critics than the film. The Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC was a historical event: 300 Spartans and their allies held a narrow pass against an invading Persian army of hundreds of thousands for three days, buying Greece enough time to mobilize. The film, adapted from Frank Miller's graphic novel, treats this as myth rather than history, and the myth is about the willingness of free men to die rather than submit. Leonidas' answer to the Persian emissary -- "This is Sparta!" -- is not diplomatic. It is a declaration of civilizational difference. The Spartans are not portrayed as saints. They are warriors in a slave-owning, eugenicist society. The film does not ask you to approve of Sparta. It asks you to understand why three hundred men would die at a mountain pass rather than kneel. +21.1 TRAD.

#16. Lost: Season 1 (2004)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 24.0 WOKE: 3.2 MARGIN: +20.8 TRAD

Director: J.J. Abrams • Stars: Matthew Fox (Jack), Evangeline Lilly (Kate), Josh Holloway (Sawyer), Terry O'Quinn (Locke) • Year: 2004

The first season of Lost was a cultural event, and its traditional underpinnings are stronger than anyone at the time appreciated. Jack Shephard is a spinal surgeon thrust into leadership of 48 plane crash survivors on a mysterious island. He does not want the job. He takes it because no one else will, and because people will die if someone does not make decisions. The flashback structure -- each episode exploring one character's pre-island life -- is a sustained argument about redemption: every person on that plane was broken in some fundamental way, and the island is their chance to become someone else. John Locke's faith that the island has a purpose, that their arrival was not random, that everything happens for a reason, is the spiritual counterweight to Jack's scientific skepticism. The season builds to a conclusion that raises more questions than it answers, but the moral architecture of the first 25 episodes is undeniable: community formed through necessity, leadership earned through competence, and the conviction that the past does not have to determine the future. +20.8 TRAD.

#17. Batman Begins (2005)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 26.0 WOKE: 5.5 MARGIN: +20.5 TRAD

Director: Christopher Nolan • Stars: Christian Bale (Bruce Wayne), Michael Caine (Alfred), Liam Neeson (Ducard), Gary Oldman (Gordon), Cillian Murphy (Scarecrow) • Year: 2005

Batman Begins rescued the Batman franchise from the camp excess of the Schumacher era by treating the character with absolute seriousness. Bruce Wayne's journey from orphaned billionaire to vigilante is framed as a quest for justice, not revenge. His training with the League of Shadows under Ra's al Ghul/Ducard forces him to confront the moral limits of his mission: the League wants him to execute a murderer as his final test. Bruce refuses. He burns the League's temple instead. The distinction -- between justice and vengeance, between becoming a symbol and becoming a killer -- is the film's moral spine. Gotham is portrayed as a city rotting from corruption, and Batman's emergence is not portrayed as a progressive disruption of institutions but as a restoration of the possibility of justice where institutions have failed. The 5.5 woke score reflects the film's limited critique of wealth and systemic corruption. But its fundamental argument -- that a man can become more than a man, a symbol that outlasts him -- is traditional through and through. +20.5 TRAD.

TRADITIONAL

#18. Click (2006)

TRADITIONAL TRAD: 20.0 WOKE: 2.0 MARGIN: +18.0 TRAD

Director: Frank Coraci • Stars: Adam Sandler (Michael), Kate Beckinsale (Donna), Christopher Walken (Morty) • Year: 2006

Click is the Adam Sandler film that nobody expected to make them cry, and it is arguably the most emotionally effective thing he has ever done. Michael Newman is a workaholic architect who acquires a universal remote control that lets him fast-forward through his life. He skips arguments with his wife. He skips illnesses. He skips family dinners. He skips everything that is not work, and when he wakes up, he is old, divorced, estranged from his children, and his father is dead. The scene in which Michael, on auto-pilot, revisits the last time he saw his father -- coldly rejecting him while focused on work -- and desperately screams at his past self to turn around and say something is Sandler's single best moment as a dramatic actor. The film's moral is devastatingly traditional: the moments you want to skip are the moments that constitute your life. Career ambition without family is a hollow victory. The remote is a Faustian bargain, and the price is everything that matters. +18.0 TRAD.

#19. Taken (2008)

TRADITIONAL TRAD: 20.3 WOKE: 2.8 MARGIN: +17.6 TRAD

Director: Pierre Morel • Stars: Liam Neeson (Bryan Mills), Maggie Grace (Kim), Famke Janssen (Lenore) • Year: 2008

Taken is the simplest film on this list, and that is its strength. Bryan Mills is a retired CIA operative whose 17-year-old daughter is kidnapped by Albanian sex traffickers in Paris. He has 96 hours to find her before she disappears forever. The film does not complicate this premise. It does not subvert it. It does not ask whether Bryan's "particular set of skills" are problematic. It presents a father who will burn down an entire criminal enterprise to save his child, and it frames this as unambiguously heroic. The famous phone call -- "I will look for you, I will find you, and I will kill you" -- is not a threat. It is a promise, delivered by a man who has spent his career making good on such promises and who does not distinguish between Albanian gangsters and anyone else who stands between him and his daughter. The film's 2.8 woke score reflects its near-total disinterest in progressive framing. +17.6 TRAD.

#20. Gran Torino (2008)

TRADITIONAL TRAD: 22.0 WOKE: 4.5 MARGIN: +17.5 TRAD

Director: Clint Eastwood • Stars: Clint Eastwood (Walt Kowalski), Bee Vang (Thao), Ahney Her (Sue) • Year: 2008

Gran Torino is Clint Eastwood's farewell to the kind of man he spent fifty years playing, and it is more complicated than either its fans or its critics acknowledge. Walt Kowalski is a retired Detroit auto worker, a Korean War veteran, a recent widower, and a racist. He growls at his Hmong neighbors. He uses slurs. He is not a nice man. But the film does not treat Walt's racism as his essence. It treats it as a surface defense erected by a man who has seen too much and lost too much, and who discovers, reluctantly, that the Hmong family next door has more traditional values -- hard work, family loyalty, respect for elders -- than his own children and grandchildren. Walt's sacrifice at the end -- allowing himself to be gunned down by the gang that has been terrorizing the neighborhood, unarmed, so they will be imprisoned and the family will be safe -- is a Christ-figure ending that Eastwood earns through two hours of character work. The film is not a redemption narrative in the progressive sense. Walt does not renounce his past or his country. He dies protecting people he has come to love, using his own death as the final tactical move. +17.5 TRAD.

#21. Cast Away (2000)

TRADITIONAL TRAD: 19.0 WOKE: 1.7 MARGIN: +17.3 TRAD

Director: Robert Zemeckis • Stars: Tom Hanks (Chuck Noland), Helen Hunt (Kelly) • Year: 2000

Cast Away is a film with almost no dialogue for its middle hour and almost no ideological content in its entire runtime, which is why it lands at +17.3 TRAD with a 1.7 woke score. Chuck Noland is a FedEx efficiency expert whose plane crashes in the South Pacific. He spends four years alone on an island, surviving through sheer determination, and the film is an extended meditation on what keeps a human being going when everything external has been stripped away. The answer is Kelly. Her picture in the locket. The promise of returning to her. When Chuck finally escapes and returns to civilization, Kelly has moved on. She is married. She has children. The scene in which Chuck tells his best friend what kept him alive -- "I had power over nothing" -- and then confronts the reality that she cannot come back to him, is the most emotionally honest resolution any blockbuster of the 2000s attempted. +17.3 TRAD.

#22. The Dark Knight (2008)

TRADITIONAL TRAD: 19.6 WOKE: 3.5 MARGIN: +16.1 TRAD

Director: Christopher Nolan • Stars: Christian Bale (Batman), Heath Ledger (Joker), Aaron Eckhart (Dent/Two-Face), Gary Oldman (Gordon) • Year: 2008

The Dark Knight is the most thematically ambitious superhero film ever made, and its TRADITIONAL verdict at +16.1 may surprise people who have read it as a post-9/11 surveillance-state critique. The Joker is not an ideologue. He is an agent of chaos who wants to prove that everyone, given the right circumstances, is one bad day away from becoming a monster. His entire scheme is designed to corrupt Gotham's white knight, Harvey Dent, and he succeeds. The film's counterargument is not that institutions are trustworthy. It is that individual character matters more. The boats sequence -- two ferries, one full of civilians and one full of prisoners, each given the detonator to the other's bomb, each refusing to use it -- is the moral climax of the entire Nolan trilogy. The killer convict throws the detonator out the window. The citizens vote but cannot bring themselves to do it. The Joker's premise is refuted. Batman's decision to take the blame for Dent's crimes, preserving Dent's legacy as a symbol while becoming a hunted fugitive himself, is the ultimate traditional sacrifice: the hero who can take it, who is not a hero in the conventional sense, who can be the villain the city needs him to be. +16.1 TRAD.
